## What this part is about

In Part 1, Ansible prepared the Lemonade Stand servers. In Part 2, k3s ran the app as the Deployment `lemonade-web` in the namespace `lemonade`. One question is still open: **how does a new version get from a programmer's laptop to the customers?**

Doing it by hand means running the tests (if you remember), building a container image, pushing it, editing a manifest and running `kubectl`, at midnight, while hoping nothing was forgotten. A **CI/CD pipeline** is a robot that does those steps the same way every time a change is pushed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Explain it like I'm ten

Think of a real lemonade stand. Before a new recipe reaches a customer, it passes a line of checkpoints: someone mixes it, someone tastes it, someone pours it into bottles with a label, a friend tries one bottle, and only then does the bottle go on the counter. If any checkpoint says "yuck", the bottle never reaches the counter. A CI/CD pipeline is that line of checkpoints for software, and a robot runs it every time anyone changes the recipe.
:::

## The Lemonade pipeline

Every lesson builds a piece of this one pipeline. Lesson 9 puts all of it together.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Commit pushed to main] --> B[Test]
  B --> C[Build and push image]
  C --> D[Deploy to staging]
  D --> E{Human approves?}
  E -->|yes| F[Deploy to production]
  B -.->|red| X[Stop and fix]
```

| Stage | What happens to the Lemonade Stand | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test | `npm test` checks the price rules and the HTTP endpoints | [4](04-automated-testing-in-the-pipeline.qmd) |
| Build image | A container image `ghcr.io/<owner>/lemonade-stand:<git-sha>` is built once and pushed | [5](05-artifacts-caching-and-versioning.qmd) |
| Deploy staging | The image goes to a practice k3s cluster | [7](07-deployment-strategies.qmd), [9](09-end-to-end-lemonade-pipeline.qmd) |
| Approval | A reviewer clicks "Approve" on the `production` environment | [6](06-secrets-environments-and-approvals.qmd) |
| Deploy production | The **same** image rolls out to the real cluster, pod by pod | [7](07-deployment-strategies.qmd), [9](09-end-to-end-lemonade-pipeline.qmd) |

## The lab

The runnable example lives in [`examples/lemonade-stand/`](examples/lemonade-stand/README.md):

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `server.mjs` | The app: one pure pricing function and a tiny HTTP handler (`/`, `/health`, `/price`) |
| `server.test.mjs` | Four tests of real behaviour, run with `node --test` |
| `Dockerfile` | A six-line image recipe on a pinned `node:26.13.1-alpine3.24` base |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | The Namespace, Deployment and Service from Part 2, with an `__IMAGE__` placeholder |
| `workflows/ci.yml` | Test, build and push, then call the deploy workflow twice |
| `workflows/deploy.yml` | A reusable deploy workflow: apply, wait for the rollout, roll back on failure |

```bash
cd devops/ci-cd/examples/lemonade-stand
npm test                      # 4 tests, no dependencies to install
PORT=8080 node server.mjs     # then: curl localhost:8080/price?classic=2
```

## Glossary

| Word | Meaning in one line |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous integration (CI) | Everyone merges small changes into the main branch often, and a robot checks every merge |
| Continuous delivery | Every change that passes the pipeline *could* be released with one button press |
| Continuous deployment | Every change that passes the pipeline *is* released, with no button |
| Pipeline / workflow | The whole list of automated checkpoints, written in a file in the repository |
| Trigger / event | What starts the pipeline: a push, a pull request, a timer, a button |
| Job | A group of steps that run together on one machine |
| Step | One command or one reusable action inside a job |
| Runner | The machine that executes a job |
| Artifact | A file the pipeline produces and keeps, such as a test report or a built package |
| Container image | A packaged app plus everything it needs to run, stored in a registry |
| Digest | The fingerprint (`sha256:...`) of an image; it never changes |
| Environment | A named deployment target such as `staging` or `production`, with its own secrets and rules |
| Secret | A password or key the pipeline needs but must never print |
| Status check | The green tick or red cross a pipeline puts on a commit or pull request |
| Rollback | Going back to the previous working version |

## Mathematical Abstraction

A pipeline is a chain of gates. A change reaches production only if it passes all of them:

$$
\operatorname{ship}(c) \iff \bigwedge_{i=1}^{k} g_i(c)
$$

where

- $c$ is one change (one commit);
- $k$ is the number of gates in the pipeline (a whole number, $k \ge 1$);
- $g_i(c)$ is true when gate number $i$ accepts change $c$, and false otherwise;
- $\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}$ means "gate 1 **and** gate 2 **and** ... **and** gate $k$";
- $\iff$ means "exactly when": both sides are true together or false together;
- $\operatorname{ship}(c)$ is true when $c$ is allowed into production.

**Example.** The Lemonade pipeline has $k = 4$ gates: $g_1$ = tests pass, $g_2$ = image builds, $g_3$ = staging rollout succeeds, $g_4$ = a reviewer approves. A commit that changes the mint price passes the tests ($g_1 = \text{true}$), builds ($g_2 = \text{true}$), rolls out to staging ($g_3 = \text{true}$), but the reviewer rejects it ($g_4 = \text{false}$). Then

$$
\operatorname{ship}(c) = \text{true} \land \text{true} \land \text{true} \land \text{false} = \text{false},
$$

so the new price never reaches customers. One "no" anywhere is enough to stop a change, which is why gates that are fast and cheap should come first (see [Lesson 4](04-automated-testing-in-the-pipeline.qmd)).
